newsitem.title: USA: Boeing-Lockheed group signs $7 billion shuttle pact.
newsitem.headline: Boeing-Lockheed group signs $7 billion shuttle pact.

text.p: A venture grouping Boeing Co. and Lockheed Martin Corp. said Monday it signed an agreement to be the prime contractor for the space shuttle programme, a deal expected to be worth about $7 billion over six years.

The Houston-based venture, United Space Alliance, was formed in August 1995 by Rockwell International Corp. and Lockheed Martin to bid on the contract with NASA, the nation's space agency. As part of Boeing's acquisition of Rockwell's aerospace and defence business, Rockwell's share of the alliance will be transferred to a unit of Boeing, pending approvals later this year, the venture said in a statement.
The contract includes responsibility for the orbiter, flight and ground operations and logistics support, and can be renewed for two two-year periods, the alliance said.
The contract is a key piece of NASA's controversial plan to place the day-to-day running of the shuttle programme in private hands as the agency seeks to cut spending.

The contract was written to include incentives to meet NASA's primary goals of maintaining mission safety and flight schedule and reducing costs, and calls for added fees for achieving mission objectives as well as significant penalties for failing to meet the objectives, it said.

"I believe we have successfully negotiated a contract with incentive provisions that will motivate us to manage the shuttle programme with the same order of priority that NASA has followed in the past -- fly our missions safely, meet mission requirements, and reduce costs," United Space Alliance Chief Executive Kent Black said in a statement.

The alliance will prepare the shuttles for flight, launch the vehicles and service them after landing. It will also train astronauts, operate the mission control centre and plan mission schedules. The work will be done at the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida and the Johnson Space Centre in Texas.
Under subcontract to the alliance, Rockwell, which builds the shuttle's orbiter and main engines, will continue to provide shuttle modifications and engineering support, the alliance said.
One of the main jobs will be to use the shuttles to help build the planned international space station, the alliance said.
It said the contract represents a new way of doing business with the government, focusing responsibilty on one contractor, and replacing 12 previous contracts.

In the second phase, work from 16 additional contracts will be brought under management of the alliance. These include contracts for the shuttle's main engines, external tanks, the solid rocket boosters and the reusable solid rocket motors.
